definition:
To sanctify is to make holy, and in the Bible to be holy is first of all to belong to God, set apart from common use for him, and then to become like him in character. Sanctification is the Holy Spirit's work of setting believers apart for God and changing them, over a lifetime, into the likeness of Jesus Christ. Scripture speaks of it in two tenses. Believers already are sanctified: Paul writes to a troubled congregation as “those sanctified in Christ Jesus and called to be holy” (1 Corinthians 1:2). And believers are being sanctified: they “are being transformed into His image with intensifying glory” (2 Corinthians 3:18). Many theologians call the first ‘definitive’ sanctification and the second ‘progressive’ sanctification, and they add a third tense, the completion at Christ's return, when “we will be like Him” (1 John 3:2). Sanctification is distinct from justification, God's verdict that sinners stand in the right before him, though the two are never separated; this study concerns the holiness of God's people, while God's own holiness and the worship it calls for have their own study.

The Hebrew root is qadash. The verb means ‘to be holy’ or, in its causative and intensive forms, ‘to consecrate’ or ‘to sanctify’; the noun qodesh means ‘holiness’ or ‘a holy thing’, and the adjective qadosh means ‘holy’. The root's origin is uncertain (some have linked it to separation, others to brightness), and its meaning is learned from how it is used: whatever is holy belongs to God's sphere. The Greek Old Testament and the New Testament use the hagios family. Hagiazō means ‘to sanctify’, ‘consecrate’, or ‘treat as holy’; hagiasmos, which occurs ten times in the New Testament, means ‘sanctification’ or ‘holiness’, often the process or its outcome (Romans 6:19, 22; 1 Thessalonians 4:3); hagiōsynē means ‘holiness’ as a quality (2 Corinthians 7:1; 1 Thessalonians 3:13); and hagios means ‘holy’. The plural hoi hagioi, ‘the holy ones’, is the New Testament's ordinary name for Christians, usually translated ‘saints’. In the Bible a saint is not a rare hero of virtue but any member of God's people.
ot:
The first thing the Bible calls holy is a day: “God blessed the seventh day and sanctified it” (Genesis 2:3). Holiness begins not as a moral achievement but as God's claim, marking something as his. At Sinai the claim extends to a people. “You will be My treasured possession out of all the nations”, God says, “And unto Me you shall be a kingdom of priests and a holy nation” (Exodus 19:5-6). Israel is holy because God chose it: “you are a people holy to the LORD your God” (Deuteronomy 7:6). The tabernacle, the priests, the altar, and the vessels were consecrated for God's service (Exodus 29:43-44), and the high priest wore a gold plate on his turban engraved “HOLY TO THE LORD” (Exodus 28:36). The sabbath was given as a sign “so that you may know that I am the LORD who sanctifies you” (Exodus 31:13).

Leviticus joins God's act and Israel's response. The same chapter commands, “Consecrate yourselves, therefore, and be holy”, and says, “I am the LORD who sanctifies you” (Leviticus 20:7-8). The holy people must become in practice what God has made them in status. The refrain of Leviticus, “be holy, because I am holy” (Leviticus 11:44-45), is set in chapter 19, at the heart of the section scholars call the Holiness Code (Leviticus 17 to 26), in the middle of ordinary life. “Be holy because I, the LORD your God, am holy” (Leviticus 19:2) opens a chapter about leaving the edges of the harvest for the poor and the foreigner, paying the hired worker the same day, refusing to curse the deaf or trip the blind, judging fairly, and ends with, “love your neighbor as yourself” (Leviticus 19:9-18). Ritual purity and moral life are woven together, and neither can be dropped. Holiness in Israel was never merely separation from the unclean; it was likeness to the God who cares for the poor.

The prophets show both how far Israel fell short and how God meant to make it holy. Isaiah sees the LORD enthroned and hears the seraphim cry, “Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of Hosts” (Isaiah 6:3). His response is not pride at being near but ruin: “I am a man of unclean lips” (Isaiah 6:5). A coal from the altar touches his lips and his sin is atoned for (Isaiah 6:7). Holiness is the gift of the Holy One before it is the task of the one made holy. Ezekiel promises that God will vindicate his holy name, profaned by Israel among the nations, by showing his holiness in his people, cleansing them, giving them a new heart, and putting his Spirit within them to “cause you to walk in My statutes” (Ezekiel 36:22-27). Sanctification will be the Spirit's work. Isaiah pictures a road called “the Way of Holiness” (Isaiah 35:8), and Zechariah ends his book with a vision in which “HOLY TO THE LORD” is inscribed even on horses' bells and every cooking pot in Jerusalem is holy (Zechariah 14:20-21): the high priest's inscription spreads to the ordinary things of daily life.

The wisdom books and the Psalms show holiness as a way of life lived before God. “How can a young man keep his way pure? By guarding it according to Your word” (Psalm 119:9). The psalmist asks God to search him and see “if there is any offensive way in me” (Psalm 139:24). Proverbs pictures growth: “The path of the righteous is like the first gleam of dawn, shining brighter and brighter until midday” (Proverbs 4:18). And Solomon's prayer is honest about the struggle: “there is no one who does not sin” (1 Kings 8:46).
nt:
Jesus sets the standard at its height: “Be perfect, therefore, as your heavenly Father is perfect” (Matthew 5:48). The word translated ‘perfect’, teleios, means complete or whole, and in context it is the love that reaches even enemies, as the Father sends rain on the just and the unjust. On the night before his death Jesus prays for his disciples, “Sanctify them by the truth; Your word is truth”, and adds, “For them I sanctify Myself, so that they too may be sanctified by the truth” (John 17:17, 19). He consecrates himself to his mission and his death, and his disciples are consecrated through his self-offering and sent into the world (John 17:18). Hebrews draws out the same link: “we have been sanctified through the sacrifice of the body of Jesus Christ once for all” (Hebrews 10:10), and “by a single offering He has made perfect for all time those who are being sanctified” (Hebrews 10:14). The verse holds both tenses together: perfected once for all, being sanctified still. In Acts, Paul commissions the Ephesian elders to the word of God's grace, which gives “an inheritance among all who are sanctified” (Acts 20:32), and he recalls Jesus sending him to the Gentiles so that they might receive “an inheritance among those sanctified by faith in Me” (Acts 26:18).

Paul writes to churches full of failure and still calls them holy. The Corinthians had factions, lawsuits, and sexual sin, and Paul tells them, “you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified, in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God” (1 Corinthians 6:11); Christ himself has become “our righteousness, holiness, and redemption” (1 Corinthians 1:30). From that status he argues to conduct. In Romans 6, answering the question whether grace permits sin, he says believers have died with Christ, and so, “Do not present the parts of your body to sin as instruments of wickedness” (Romans 6:13); they have been set free from sin and “the fruit you reap leads to holiness” (Romans 6:22). Romans 7:14-25 describes a person who delights in God's law but finds “another law at work in my body, warring against the law of my mind” (Romans 7:23). Whether this ‘I’ is Paul the mature Christian, as Augustine in his later writings, Luther, and Calvin held, or a person under the law without the Spirit, as Werner Georg Kümmel argued in 1929 and many modern scholars follow, remains one of the most debated questions in Romans. Romans 8 then describes the Spirit's work: “if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live” (Romans 8:13), and God's purpose is that his people be “conformed to the image of His Son” (Romans 8:29). The believer offers his body as “living sacrifices, holy and pleasing to God” and is to “be transformed by the renewing of your mind” (Romans 12:1-2). The verb, metamorphoō, is the one used of Jesus' transfiguration, and Paul uses it again in 2 Corinthians 3:18, where believers beholding the Lord's glory are transformed “into His image with intensifying glory, which comes from the Lord, who is the Spirit”.

Several passages show how God's work and the believer's effort relate. “Continue to work out your salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God who works in you to will and to act on behalf of His good purpose” (Philippians 2:12-13): the believer works because God works, not instead of him. Galatians sets the Spirit against the flesh (Paul's word for human nature in its fallen self-reliance) and calls believers to “walk by the Spirit”, and the result is not many fruits but one, “the fruit of the Spirit”, which is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control (Galatians 5:16, 22-23). Ephesians and Colossians speak of putting off the old self and putting on the new (Ephesians 4:22-24; Colossians 3:9-10). Paul is frank that he has not arrived: “Not that I have already obtained all this, or have already been made perfect, but I press on” (Philippians 3:12). Holiness is concrete: “it is God's will that you should be holy: You must abstain from sexual immorality”, and no one should “violate or exploit his brother” (1 Thessalonians 4:3, 6). And it is finally God's own work: “may the God of peace Himself sanctify you completely”, for “The One who calls you is faithful, and He will do it” (1 Thessalonians 5:23-24). The Spirit is named as the agent: God chose believers “to be saved by the sanctification of the Spirit and by faith in the truth” (2 Thessalonians 2:13).

The other apostolic writers agree. Hebrews presents God's discipline as a father's training, “so that we may share in His holiness” (Hebrews 12:10), and urges believers to pursue “holiness, without which no one will see the Lord” (Hebrews 12:14). Peter writes to believers “sanctified by the Spirit for obedience to Jesus Christ” (1 Peter 1:2) and quotes Leviticus: “Be holy, because I am holy” (1 Peter 1:16). Second Peter calls believers to “make every effort” to add virtue to faith (2 Peter 1:5) and to “grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ” (2 Peter 3:18). John holds together honesty and hope: “If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves”, but “If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:8-9). The end is sure: “when Christ appears, we will be like Him”, and “everyone who has this hope in Him purifies himself” (1 John 3:2-3). Christ gave himself for the church “to sanctify her” and to present her “holy and blameless” (Ephesians 5:26-27).

keyTexts.why: Israel is called to be a kingdom of priests and a holy nation. Holiness begins with God's choosing and claiming a people for himself.
Be holy because God is holy, followed by laws about the poor, wages, honesty, justice, and love of neighbor. Holiness reaches into ordinary social life.
God shows his holiness by cleansing his people and putting his Spirit within them to walk in his ways. The promise that sanctification will be the Spirit's work.
Jesus asks the Father to sanctify his disciples by the truth and consecrates himself for their sake. Their holiness flows from his self-offering.
Believers freed from sin become slaves of righteousness, and the fruit leads to holiness. Grace is not permission to sin but the power of a new master.
Believers offer their bodies as living sacrifices and are transformed by the renewing of the mind. Sanctification involves the body, the mind, and resistance to the world's pattern.
People once defined by sin were washed, sanctified, and justified. Definitive sanctification is spoken to a congregation still struggling.
Beholding the Lord's glory, believers are transformed into his image by the Spirit. Growth comes through seeing Christ.
The Spirit and the flesh are opposed, and the Spirit produces a single fruit of love and its companions. The Christian life is lived by walking in step with the Spirit.
Work out your salvation, for God works in you to will and to act. The classic text for how divine grace and human effort relate.
God's will is your sanctification, including sexual purity and refusal to wrong others. Holiness is concrete and rejecting it is rejecting God.
Believers are sanctified once for all through Christ's sacrifice and are being sanctified. Both tenses of sanctification stand in one passage.
God disciplines his children so they may share his holiness, and without holiness no one will see the Lord. Hardship is one of the means of growth.
Peter applies Leviticus's call to be holy as God is holy to Christians. The Old Testament standard carries into the new covenant.
When Christ appears, we will be like him, and this hope purifies. Sanctification is completed in glorification.

history:
The early church understood the Christian life as a life of holiness begun in baptism. The Didache, a church manual from about the late first or early second century, opens with the ‘two ways’ of life and death, and early baptismal instruction prepared converts to renounce their old life. The desert monks of Egypt, beginning with Antony (about 251 to 356), pursued holiness through prayer, fasting, and struggle against the passions, and their sayings shaped Christian spirituality in East and West. Gregory of Nyssa, in his Life of Moses (late fourth century), described perfection not as a fixed state but as endless growth into God, since God is infinite. Augustine, against Pelagius, taught that holiness is itself a gift of grace, God's love poured into the heart by the Spirit (Romans 5:5), and that no one in this life is without sin. The Council of Carthage (418) condemned the claim that the saints pray “forgive us our debts” (Matthew 6:12) only out of humility and not because it is true of them. Medieval theology, summed up by Thomas Aquinas, described sanctifying grace as a habit infused into the soul, growing through the sacraments and good works done in grace, with purification completed after death for those who need it. The Council of Vienne (1311 to 1312) condemned the claim that a person in this life can reach a perfection in which he can no longer sin or grow in grace. The Imitation of Christ, attributed to Thomas à Kempis in the early fifteenth century, became the most widely read book of devotion after the Bible.

The Reformers reframed holiness as the fruit of justification, not its ground. Martin Luther, in his lectures on Romans (1515 to 1516), described the believer as at the same time righteous and a sinner (simul iustus et peccator), righteous in Christ and still fighting sin in himself; in the 1530s he opposed Johann Agricola, who taught that the law had no place in the Christian life, in the Antinomian disputations and in Against the Antinomians (1539). John Calvin taught that union with Christ brings a double grace of justification and sanctification (Institutes 3.11.1) and treated the Christian life as lifelong repentance and self-denial (3.3 and 3.7). The Heidelberg Catechism (1563) treats the Christian life of obedience under the heading of gratitude and says that even the holiest make only a small beginning of obedience in this life (question 114). The Lutheran Formula of Concord (1577, Article VI) affirmed a third use of the law as a guide for the regenerate. The Westminster Confession (1646, chapter 13) describes sanctification as extending to the whole person yet imperfect in this life, with a continual war between the flesh and the Spirit in which the regenerate part overcomes through Christ's Spirit. Rome, at the Council of Trent (Session VI, 1547), taught that the justified increase in the righteousness they have received by keeping God's commandments, cooperating with grace. John Owen's Of the Mortification of Sin in Believers (1656) became a classic on Romans 8:13, and Philipp Jakob Spener's Pia Desideria (1675) launched German Pietism's call for a living, practical holiness.

John Wesley made holiness the great theme of Methodism. In A Plain Account of Christian Perfection (1766) he taught that believers may, in this life, be made perfect in love, freed from willful transgression of known law though not from ignorance, mistakes, or infirmity, a gift received by faith, often instantaneously, after a gradual work. The nineteenth-century Holiness movement developed this teaching; Phoebe Palmer's The Way of Holiness (1843) taught a ‘shorter way’ of entire consecration and faith, and churches such as the Church of the Nazarene (1908) grew from it. The Keswick Convention in England, begun in 1875, taught a ‘higher life’ of victory over sin by surrender and faith, popularized in Hannah Whitall Smith's The Christian's Secret of a Happy Life (1875). J. C. Ryle's Holiness (1877, enlarged 1879) answered with an older Reformed account of holiness as a lifelong fight, and B. B. Warfield's two volumes on Perfectionism (published after his death, 1931 to 1932) criticized the perfectionist movements. Early Pentecostals largely held a Holiness view of sanctification as a second work of grace, until William Durham's 1910 teaching of the ‘finished work of Calvary’ located sanctification in conversion and ongoing growth, a view the Assemblies of God (founded 1914) adopted. In the twentieth century John Murray's essay Definitive Sanctification (1967) recovered the New Testament's past-tense language, and two volumes, Five Views on Sanctification (1987) and Christian Spirituality: Five Views of Sanctification (1988), set the Protestant positions side by side. The Orthodox churches continued to speak of the Christian life as theosis, growth in likeness to God through prayer, sacraments, and ascetic struggle, a tradition gathered in the Philokalia (1782).

differ.view: The Reformed view: definitive and progressive
differ.body: Reformed theology teaches that every believer has been decisively set apart by union with Christ in his death and resurrection, so that sin no longer reigns (Romans 6), and that the Spirit then renews the whole person gradually throughout life, putting sin to death and bringing the new self to life. The renewed will truly cooperates, but only because God works in it (Philippians 2:12-13). The law of God, fulfilled in love, guides the grateful believer. Sanctification is never complete in this life; the struggle of Romans 7, read as the Christian's experience, continues until death. God uses ordinary means: the word, the sacraments, prayer, the fellowship of the church, and discipline. Defenders include Calvin, the Westminster Confession, John Owen, J. C. Ryle, John Murray, and Anthony Hoekema.

differ.view: The Lutheran view: living from justification
differ.body: Lutherans hold that sanctification is the fruit of justification, the life that springs from faith in the forgiveness of sins, and that the believer remains simul iustus et peccator until death. Progress is real, but it is not the ground of confidence, and focusing on one's own progress easily becomes a new form of self-justification. The Christian life is a daily return to baptism: the old self drowned in repentance, the new self rising in faith. Good works flow freely toward the neighbor, who needs them, rather than toward God, who does not. The Formula of Concord affirms that the law guides believers; some modern Lutheran theologians, Gerhard Forde among them, press the point that sanctification is simply justification taking hold of a person, and caution against any program of holiness that turns attention from Christ to the self.

Wesleyan and Holiness churches teach that after the new birth begins sanctification, God can, in this life, so fill the believer with love for God and neighbor that the heart is cleansed from inward sin and the will is wholly given to God. This entire sanctification, or Christian perfection, is not sinless perfection: it leaves ignorance, mistakes, temptation, and the need of Christ's atonement, and it can be lost and must grow. It is received by faith, often in a distinct moment after conversion. Defenders point to 1 Thessalonians 5:23-24, where God will sanctify completely, to Matthew 5:48, to 1 John 3:9, and to the conviction that God's commands are also promises; they hold that setting the bar lower than Scripture sets it limits what grace can do.

differ.view: The Keswick or Higher Life view
differ.body: The Keswick teaching, influential in evangelical missions and conventions since 1875, holds that many Christians live defeated lives because they try to overcome sin in their own strength. By a decisive act of surrender and faith, believers can enter a life of consistent victory in which the indwelling Christ, by his Spirit, counteracts the sinful nature, which is not eradicated but is held in check as the believer abides in him. Growth continues after this crisis. Defenders such as J. Robertson McQuilkin appeal to Romans 6:11-13, Galatians 2:20, and John 15:4-5, and argue that the New Testament promises more victory than many churches expect.

differ.view: Catholic and Orthodox views: growth in grace and theosis
differ.body: Roman Catholic teaching does not separate sanctification from justification: justification itself includes the inward renewal of the person by sanctifying grace, which grows through the sacraments, prayer, and good works done in grace, which God rewards as his own gifts. Venial sins do not destroy this grace; mortal sin does, and it is restored through repentance and the sacrament of penance; purification may be completed after death. The Orthodox churches speak of theosis, a lifelong growth by grace into likeness to God through the sacraments, prayer, and ascetic struggle against the passions, in synergy with the Spirit. Both traditions honor the saints as witnesses that such growth is real, and both read 2 Peter 1:4 and 2 Corinthians 3:18 as describing the heart of the Christian life.

errors:
The church has rejected distortions on both sides. Antinomianism, from the Greek for ‘against law’, holds that because believers are under grace, how they live does not matter or that God's commands no longer apply to them. Paul answered it in Romans 6 (“Shall we sin because we are not under law, but under grace? Certainly not!”), Luther opposed it in his disputes with Agricola, and Reformed and Wesleyan confessions all reject it. Legalism, or moralism, errs the other way, treating holiness as the way to earn or keep God's favor, or reducing it to a list of external rules; Paul's letter to the Galatians, Jesus' conflict with the Pharisees over washings and sabbaths, and the Reformation's insistence that good works are the fruit and not the root of salvation all stand against it. Perfectionism claims a sinless state reachable in this life. The Council of Carthage (418) and the Council of Vienne (1311 to 1312) rejected forms of it, and 1 John 1:8 warns that those who say they have no sin deceive themselves; Wesleyans carefully distinguish their teaching of perfect love from any claim to sinlessness.

Other errors are subtler. Quietism, associated with Miguel de Molinos and condemned by Pope Innocent XI in 1687, taught a passivity in which the soul should cease striving and even resisting temptation; Scripture calls believers both to rest in God's work and to make every effort (Philippians 2:12-13; 2 Peter 1:5). Holiness can also be shrunk to private piety, cut off from the justice and neighbor-love that Leviticus 19 places at its center, or to a matter of separation from outsiders, when Jesus' holiness sent him to eat with sinners. And sanctification can be made into a program of self-improvement that uses Christian words but relies on willpower and technique, forgetting that the New Testament calls it the work of the Spirit and the fruit of union with Christ.
life:
Sanctification means that a Christian can take both sin and grace seriously at the same time. Because believers are already set apart and loved, their failures do not undo their standing, and they can face sin honestly rather than hiding it. Because God intends to make them like Christ, they cannot make peace with their sin either. The ordinary means are unremarkable: reading and hearing Scripture, prayer, confession, the Lord's Supper, the company of other believers, and faithfulness in small duties. Hebrews adds hardship, God's discipline that is painful at the time but later yields “a harvest of righteousness and peace” (Hebrews 12:11). Growth is often slow and more visible to others than to oneself, and the fruit Paul names is mostly relational: patience, kindness, gentleness, self-control.

Holiness in Scripture is not withdrawal from ordinary life but God's claim spreading into it, like the cooking pots Zechariah saw inscribed “HOLY TO THE LORD”. It appears in how a person pays workers, treats the disabled, speaks of others, handles sexuality, and forgives. And it rests on a promise. The one who began the work will finish it (Philippians 1:6), and on the day Christ appears, his people will be like him. Christians press on not to earn that day but because it is coming.
questions: Leviticus 19 places the command to be holy beside laws about harvests, wages, the disabled, and justice. What does that chapter suggest holiness looks like in ordinary life today?

Paul calls the Corinthians ‘sanctified’ while correcting serious sin among them (1 Corinthians 1:2; 6:11). How do the two tenses of sanctification, already set apart and still being changed, help a believer who is discouraged by failure?

Philippians 2:12-13 says to work out your salvation because God works in you. How do the Christian traditions described above each understand that verse, and which misreading of it are you most tempted by?
